                                     PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                         §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                    §                   OF TEXAS


                   COMMENTS OF BLACK MOUNTAIN POWER, LLC

                                     I.    INTRODUCTION

       Black Mountain Power, LLC (“Black Mountain”) is a private, entrepreneurial energy,

power, and natural resources company with extensive experience in sourcing, developing, and

operating projects across these thematics in both the United States and Australia. Black

Mountain has transacted on more than $2 billion of projects over 18 years, and one of Black

Mountain’s business units has originated as lead developer over 3.5 GW of energy storage

projects across Texas. We are currently developing more than 15 data center projects across the

ERCOT region.

       Black Mountain understands the need to differentiate between viable and speculative

loads requesting interconnection in ERCOT, and welcomes it. It is critical, however, that this is

done in a way that does not bar credible large load developers with a history of successful

investments in Texas from development by setting unnecessarily high costs.

       We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the large load interconnection standard

rulemaking and look forward to working collaboratively with commission staff, ERCOT utilities,

and ERCOT.
                             II.   DISCUSSION DRAFT FEEDBACK

Financial Security:

       The most concerning aspect of the proposed language is the $50,000/MW security

requirement as suggested in §25.194(e)(8) of the staff’s discussion draft. The proposed collateral

requirement is excessive and risks undermining the purpose of ensuring that only well-

capitalized projects populate the queue. While the intent is to discourage speculative filings, this

level of obligation imposes a prohibitive burden that deters serious developers alongside less

viable entrants. More measured proposals, such as a ceiling of $10,000/MW, would achieve the

same objective without discouraging investment in projects with genuine potential.

       To illustrate the impact, our organization is currently advancing more than 15 data center

projects across ERCOT. Under the proposed framework, we would be required to post over $750

million in collateral simply to determine whether any of these projects could reach energization.

With cost of capital in the low teens, this translates into $80–100 million annually in interest

and carrying costs, an untenable burden with no guarantee of process, timing, or outcome. Such

requirements would inevitably lead to widespread cancellations, as no developer can justify

immobilizing this scale of funding absent certainty in study results or repayment timelines.

       SB6 must balance the dual goals of encouraging broad economic development and

ensuring the seriousness of load filings. Overemphasis on one objective at the expense of the

other risks prematurely eliminating viable projects due to cost concerns. Our track record

underscores this point: Black Mountain has transacted on more than $2 billion of projects over

18 years and our Energy Storage team has originated 3.5 GW of energy storage projects across

Texas, directly contributing to grid resiliency and reliability. Yet even with this level of
 sophistication and demonstrated commitment, the proposed deposit fees would effectively

preclude our ability to develop data center projects in Texas.

       Excessive collateral requirements risk driving away capable developers alongside

speculative entrants. A more balanced, reasonable approach would preserve the integrity of the

queue, while sustaining investment in projects that strengthen the grid and advance economic

development. Texas should not inadvertently deter high-quality projects by imposing

requirements that eliminate the good with the bad.

In-Flight Projects:

       The proposed language does not clearly address how new requirements would apply to

projects that have already initiated load interconnection studies, commonly referred to as

“in‑flight” projects. Black Mountain currently has multiple projects in this category and has

already committed substantial capital to interconnecting utilities to begin large‑load

interconnection assessments. At present, it remains unclear whether the CIAC requirement will

apply retroactively or whether a $/MW security will be imposed on these projects.

       It is essential that the Commission establish clear rules governing the treatment of

in‑flight projects. Specifically, the Commission should provide a definitive cut‑off date or filing

milestone to determine which projects are subject to the new requirements. These projects should

also not be subject to further delays and unnecessarily restudied multiple times.

       In addition, Black Mountain believes that filing sequence, meaning the timeline in which

projects submitted their interconnection requests, must be considered to avoid

disenfranchisement. Projects that filed earlier and have advanced further in the study process

should not be disadvantaged relative to later entrants. Recognizing filing sequence as a factor

would ensure fairness, protect prior investments, and maintain confidence in the integrity of the
 interconnection process. Black Mountain believes quarterly, or at most semi-annual, batches of

qualified projects with similar filing chronology is appropriate.

Site Control:

       The language in the draft proposal requires site control for at least 50% of the expected

time for the entity to reach its peak ramp before the interconnection study is complete. In

practice, this is not a common expectation for the majority of development projects. Typically,

developers do not secure full tract ownership prior to confirming the availability of power, and

most landowners are unwilling to grant long-term options extending four or five years.

       It’s critical that commission staff understand that this is not common practice in project

development, and many viable projects would unnecessarily be forced to withdraw their request

due to the inability to satisfy this specific requirement.
                                  III.   CONCLUSION

We greatly appreciate the Commission staff’s work on this issue and consideration of our

perspective.

                                               Respectfully submitted,

                                               /s/ Rhett Bennett         _
                                               Rhett Bennett
                                               Chief Executive Officer
                                               Black Mountain Power, LLC
                                   PROJECT NO. 58481

LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                    §
STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                  §                      OF TEXAS


        EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF BLACK MOUNTAIN POWER, LLC

 ● Black Mountain believes the proposed $50,000/MW collateral requirement is excessive,

    creates prohibitive burdens, and risks deterring serious developers. Black Mountain

    proposes a more reasonable ceiling of $10,000/MW.

 ● Excessive collateral requirements will drive away capable developers. A balanced

    approach is needed to preserve queue integrity while sustaining investment.

 ● Black Mountain stresses that the current language fails to clarify how requirements apply

    to “in‑flight” projects already undergoing studies. Clear guidance is essential for fairness.

 ● Black Mountain believes that requiring site control for 50% of the ramp period before

    study completion is impractical. Developers typically secure land only after confirming

    power availability, and long‑term options are rarely feasible.

 ● Black Mountain encourages Commission staff to balance economic burden with the

    seriousness of load filings. Overemphasis on collateral risks eliminating viable projects

    and undermining Texas’s ability to attract investment and strengthen resiliency.

 ● Black Mountain has demonstrated through years of successful development that we have

    a track record of successful execution. We are an example of how excessive requirements

    for collateral would increase costs of successful developers, exceedingly impair market

    access and participation, and ultimately lead to less successful data center developments

    in Texas.
